probes.what: the act opens

probes.name: L0001
probes.what: The afternoon of 15 January 1919. Boston's North End, Commercial Street.

probes.name: L0002
probes.what: From a giant tank, 2,300,000 gallons of molasses poured into the streets.

probes.name: L0003
probes.what: The next day's Boston Post reported the wave as 50 feet high; that figure is disputed.

probes.name: L0004
probes.what: By midnight, the paper counted 11 dead and more than 50 injured.

probes.name: L0005
probes.what: Sweet, thick molasses. How could it kill anyone?

probes.name: L0006
probes.what: The answer lies in a newspaper of that time, and in the city's account written a century later.

probes.name: L0007
probes.what: The story begins with a giant tank standing on Commercial Street.

probes.name: L0008
probes.what: According to the City of Boston's account, the tank was built in 1915 by the Purity Distilling Company.

probes.name: L0009
probes.what: According to the city, it was 50 feet tall and held about 2.3 million gallons of molasses.

probes.name: L0010
probes.what: The Boston Post printed the same quantity in its report: 2,300,000 gallons.

probes.name: L0011
probes.what: So on this figure, the newspaper of the time and the city's later account agree.

probes.name: L0012
probes.what: The city's account records one more thing.

probes.name: L0013
probes.what: The tank, it is reported, had been leaking before the disaster.

probes.name: L0014
probes.what: It was something like a warning sign.

probes.name: L0015
probes.what: 15 January 1919, after midday. The tank gave way.

probes.name: L0016
probes.what: According to the City of Boston, several causes came together.

probes.name: L0017
probes.what: Weak construction, changes in temperature, and a large shipment of molasses.

probes.name: L0018
probes.what: According to the Boston Post, the molasses spread over Commercial Street and its waterfront.

probes.name: L0019
probes.what: From Charter Street to the southern end of North End Park.

probes.name: L0020
probes.what: According to the city's account, the wave moved at about 35 miles an hour.

probes.name: L0021
probes.what: How high the wave was is disputed: the sources do not agree.

probes.name: L0022
probes.what: The Post wrote 50 feet, about as tall as the tank is in the city's account.

probes.name: L0023
probes.what: According to many later accounts, it was much lower.

probes.name: L0024
probes.what: In the Post's words, the sticky flood caught more than 100 men, women and children.

probes.name: L0025
probes.what: Buildings, horse teams, motor cars and streetcars. Whatever stood in its path was crushed.

probes.name: L0026
probes.what: The elevated railway structure overhead did not survive either.

probes.name: L0027
probes.what: The paper wrote that the black, reeking mass struck the buildings facing Copp's Hill.

probes.name: L0028
probes.what: And then swept back towards the harbour.

probes.name: L0029
probes.what: Among the dead was an engineer of Engine 31 of the Boston Fire Department.

probes.name: L0030
probes.what: The Post printed his name as George Lahey.

probes.name: L0031
probes.what: Among the dead was also a girl of about 14, still unidentified when the paper went to press.

probes.name: L0032
probes.what: She wore a grey jacket, and her bag carried an employment tag of the Revere Rubber Company.

probes.name: L0033
probes.what: Ambulances were rushed to the scene from every part of the city.

probes.name: L0034
probes.what: Rescue work went on at the North End Park playground.

probes.name: L0035
probes.what: Dead horses, cats and dogs were carted away, load after load.

probes.name: L0036
probes.what: Boston's only trolley freight terminal lay in ruins.

probes.name: L0037
probes.what: The Post's first count was 11 dead: a woman, a girl and nine men.

probes.name: L0038
probes.what: But the number did not stop there.

probes.name: L0039
probes.what: According to the City of Boston, 21 people died in the end, and about 150 were injured.

probes.name: L0040
probes.what: Now the biggest question: how did it happen?

probes.name: L0041
probes.what: The next day, the Boston Post reported that the state police chemist, W. L. Wedger, had reached a positive conclusion.

probes.name: L0042
probes.what: According to him, the tank had not collapsed; there had been an explosion inside it.

probes.name: L0043
probes.what: That was the early, disputed theory of the time. Later findings pointed another way.

probes.name: L0044
probes.what: According to the city's account, structural engineers later found that the tank's walls were too thin.

probes.name: L0045
probes.what: And that its material was prone to cracking.

probes.name: L0046
probes.what: According to the city's account, in 1925 a court-appointed auditor held the owners' negligence responsible.

probes.name: L0047
probes.what: So, unlike the explosion claimed on the first day, the later findings point to the tank's construction and to negligence.

probes.name: L0048
probes.what: The front page of the same newspaper carried another story.

probes.name: L0049
probes.what: The Prohibition amendment had been ratified by 35 states, and just one more was needed.

probes.name: L0050
probes.what: The molasses wave and Prohibition: both stories ran side by side on one page.

probes.name: L0051
probes.what: This film claims no link between them; just the same day, the same page.

probes.name: L0052
probes.what: On the first day, the Post wrote that the molasses had been released in some manner yet unexplained.

probes.name: L0053
probes.what: Later, the causes were recorded: walls too thin and, according to the auditor, the owners' negligence.

probes.name: L0054
probes.what: The cost of that afternoon: 21 lives.

probes.name: L0055
probes.what: This wave of molasses is a reminder of how much it matters to inspect the structures a city trusts.

probes.name: probe_close
probes.what: the act's last frame
